Lessons.Title: Cubic Units of Measure
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: select and interpret an appropriately sized standard cubic unit for real objects, then find rectangular-prism volume with labeled length dimensions. A number such as 24 without a unit is incomplete: twenty-four cubic centimeters, inches and feet describe different spaces.

Warm-up: compare a cubic foot with a cubic yard using familiar objects. Explain why the same count of differently sized cubes cannot describe the same physical volume. Describe the size of a unit cube in terms of the length of one edge.

Activity 1 — choose units: consider a juice box, lunch box, freezer, moving truck and classroom. Which of cubic centimeter, cubic inch and cubic foot would give a useful magnitude? Multiple choices can be defended with an appropriate reason and context; do not score a single unit choice as universally correct.

Activity 2 — information-gap: your partner has the missing width of a rectangular freezer. The available dimensions are length 4 feet and height 3 feet. Ask exactly what additional measurement is needed; once a width of 2 feet is supplied in the first-party model, calculate 4 × 2 × 3 = 24 cubic feet. Explain what makes a question useful, and why multiplying before obtaining the width would be an unjustified guess.

Assessment: a numeric final volume can be checked exactly when all dimensions are known, but choices of units, questions asked, and mathematical justification need teacher review. This public 2021 source lesson explicitly uses an information-gap partner routine; its publisher materials are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cubic unit
KeyConcepts.Definition: Volume of a cube with edges one unit long in the given linear unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm gives a cubic centimeter; 1 ft × 1 ft × 1 ft gives a cubic foot.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 2-foot by 3-foot by 4-foot box holds 24 cubic feet.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choosing the measurement scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: A useful cubic unit depends on the size of the object and the desired precision.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Name the cubic unit explicitly when reporting volume; do not interchange units with unequal cube edge lengths.
KeyConcepts.Example: A classroom volume is commonly expressed in cubic feet, not cubic centimeters.

KeyConcepts.Title: Information-gap measurement
KeyConcepts.Definition: A missing perpendicular dimension prevents a unique rectangular-prism volume calculation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For V = length × width × height, know all three dimensions or base area and height before calculating.
KeyConcepts.Example: A freezer 4 feet long and 3 feet high needs its width to determine the volume.

WorkedExamples.Title: Choose a practical unit
WorkedExamples.Question: Would cubic centimeters or cubic feet be more convenient to measure the volume of a large moving truck?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare the unit cube sizes with the object.
Steps: A cubic centimeter has a 1-centimeter edge, tiny relative to a truck.
A cubic foot has a 1-foot edge and describes a much larger block of space.
Choose cubic feet as a reasonable, readable unit; other units are mathematically convertible but less convenient.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Cubic feet are a sensible choice.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the object-size explanation, not merely the chosen word.

WorkedExamples.Title: Ask the missing information
WorkedExamples.Question: A freezer measures 4 feet long and 3 feet high; what else must you know to find its volume?
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify which dimension is absent from length × width × height.
Steps: List the two known perpendicular dimensions: 4 feet and 3 feet.
Note that different widths would yield different volumes.
Ask for the width or equivalent base area.
WorkedExamples.Check: There is not yet a unique numerical volume; do not invent it.

WorkedExamples.Title: Finish an information gap
WorkedExamples.Question: The freezer is 4 feet long, 2 feet wide and 3 feet high. Find its volume.
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply perpendicular side lengths using feet consistently.
Steps: Calculate base area 4 × 2 = 8 square feet.
Multiply by the matching height of 3 feet.
Give the answer as a three-dimensional unit.
WorkedExamples.Check: 8 square feet × 3 feet = 24 cubic feet.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The number alone does not specify the size of the measuring unit.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Attach cubic feet, cubic inches or cubic centimeters as appropriate to the given dimensions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Infer a missing width without asking
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The volume of a rectangular prism is not unique from only two side lengths.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Ask for the missing perpendicular dimension and justify why it is needed.

SummaryPoints: Different standard cubic units have different physical sizes.
Select a unit that makes sense for an object's scale and report it with the numerical volume.
Information-gap communication and defensible unit choices are teacher-reviewed; not every part is a fixed-response computation.

Lessons.Title: Figures Made of Prisms
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: find the volume of a solid composed of two or more non-overlapping rectangular prisms. Compare physical constructions and explain why the total space occupied equals the sum of volumes of the separate parts.

Warm-up: use a first-party collection of imagined composite solids and discuss which might be decomposed into two rectangular boxes. Different justified Which One Doesn't Belong choices are possible; do not substitute a single predetermined classification.

Activity 1 — put two prisms together: two classmates each build a right rectangular prism from equal unit cubes, bring the solids together without overlapping cube interiors, and show how their individual volumes add. As an example, 12 cubes and 10 cubes make a 22-cube composite regardless of arrangement.

Activity 2 — I see two prisms: a composite has one block 3 × 2 × 2 and another 3 × 2 × 3 joined at a face; their volumes 12 and 18 sum to 30 cubic units. Provide two possible decompositions or compare the sum to counting equal cube layers in the whole. Make the spatial arrangement explicit with accessible verbal descriptions.

Assessment boundary: a numeric sum is necessary but not sufficient when the source asks learners to construct or explain how the parts form the figure. Teacher checks the construction and whether the alleged pieces overlap. Actual publisher figure cards and restricted Cool-down are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Composite solid
KeyConcepts.Definition: A figure constructed from multiple three-dimensional solids.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Decompose into non-overlapping rectangular prisms, count each and add.
KeyConcepts.Example: A twelve-cube prism and a ten-cube prism can form a 22-cube compound solid.

KeyConcepts.Title: Additivity of volume
KeyConcepts.Definition: Total cubic-unit count equals the sum of counts of disjoint solid parts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If volumes V1 and V2 occupy non-overlapping spaces, Vtotal = V1 + V2.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 12-cube piece plus an 18-cube piece occupies 30 cubes.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiple decompositions
KeyConcepts.Definition: One solid may be partitioned into equivalent disjoint parts in different ways.
KeyConcepts.Rule: All valid partitions cover the original solid exactly once.
KeyConcepts.Example: Six 5-cube layers or two rectangular prisms of 12 and 18 may represent the same volume.

WorkedExamples.Title: Join two cube models
WorkedExamples.Question: Jada builds a 12-cube prism and Diego builds a separate 10-cube prism. What is the new volume if the solids meet only along faces?
WorkedExamples.Method: Add non-overlapping volumes.
Steps: Count twelve cubes in the first piece.
Count ten in the second; touching faces contribute no additional cubic-unit volume.
WorkedExamples.Check: The physical pieces share no cube interiors.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two right rectangular prisms
WorkedExamples.Question: One part is 3 × 2 × 2 cubes and the other 3 × 2 × 3. What is their combined volume?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute each prism volume and add.
Steps: Find first volume: 3 × 2 × 2 = 12.
Find second volume: 3 × 2 × 3 = 18.
WorkedExamples.Check: A teacher checks the attachment has no overlap; counting the full five-layer 3×2 prism also gives 6×5=30.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check overlapping counts
WorkedExamples.Question: A drawn composite has volumes 20 and 16 if treated as two boxes, but the descriptions include four of the same cubes in both pieces. What is the actual union volume?
WorkedExamples.Method: Subtract the common cubes or choose a disjoint partition.
Steps: Add the putative volumes to obtain 36.
Identify four cubes counted in both groups.
Remove one repeated count of those four cubes.
WorkedExamples.Check: 20 + 16 − 4 = 32; a non-overlapping partition gives the same total.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Overlapping parts cannot be added as though disjoint.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Create a non-overlapping decomposition or subtract the overlap once.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignore a small attached cube row
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Every cube in the solid contributes space, even if a standard large prism occupies most of it.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count each attached component as an additional non-overlapping volume.

SummaryPoints: Volume is additive for disjoint rectangular prisms.
Different partitions can count the same cubic units without altering the result.
Teacher reviews original physical construction, decomposition and explanations beyond a numeric sum.

Lessons.Title: Measure Figures Made From Prisms
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal (2021 first edition): determine composite solid volumes when individual unit cubes are NOT shown. Use given length measurements to infer missing edges, then explicitly connect each parenthesized expression to a non-overlapping rectangular-prism decomposition. Unit labels, drawing interpretation and partner justification matter.
Warm-up — Times Ten Number Talk: explain 6×2=12, 6×2×10=120, 6×20×10=1200 and 60×20×10=12000. Discuss the changing factors rather than treating a multiplication by ten as a volume unit.

Activity 1 — partner figures. Source Figure 1 describes a 7-foot horizontal length, 7-foot overall height, a 5-foot right-hand height, a 5-foot right-hand horizontal section and a 2-foot depth. Therefore the remaining lengths in those same directions are 7−5=2 feet. An original equivalent solid can be cut as (2×7×2)+(5×5×2)=28+50=78 cubic feet, or as (7×5×2)+(2×2×2)=70+8=78 cubic feet. Explain both valid non-overlapping partitions and do not substitute '78 cubic units' for its required feet-cubed unit.

Activity 1 — the second measured solid has depth 7 inches, a 9-inch upper span, a 5-inch lower span, a 5-inch total height and a 2-inch lower level; the overhang is 9−5=4 inches and upper level is 5−2=3 inches. Slice into top 9×3×7 and bottom 5×2×7 for 189+70=259 cubic inches, or left 5×5×7 and upper overhang 4×3×7 for 175+84=259 cubic inches. Partners should obtain the same total from DIFFERENT cuts and show how the parts cover the same whole without overlap.

Activity 2 — interpret the published parenthesized volume expressions, including ((2×3)×4)+((3×3)×2)=42 and (5×6)+(3×4)=42 cubic units. For the more explicitly measured composite figure, verify (5×8×6)+(5×4×9)=420 and (5×4×3)+(5×12×6)=420 cubic inches. The first 420 expression cuts vertical pieces (right 8-by-6 and left 4-by-9 with common 5-inch depth); the second cuts a full 12-by-6 lower layer and a 4-by-3 upper extension. A numeric equality by itself does NOT prove a student's partition matches the particular diagram.

Academic/Practice boundary: the 2021 teacher directions require partners to exchange figure solutions and use different decompositions, infer missing lengths, justify an expression's parentheses and specify cubic feet versus cubic inches. Numeric positives/negatives and 2D cell-union models support Practice, but teacher must evaluate student drawings, unit interpretation and explanation. The public teacher lesson and preparation HTML with embedded Student Facing text were read read-only on approved Our-CS; separate Student Task PDF, original publisher figures/cards and gated Cool-down were NOT verified or copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Find missing edges from labeled geometry
KeyConcepts.Definition: A composite prism may have a known overall extent plus a segment length in the same direction; subtract to determine the unknown length.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 7−5=2 feet for the first source shape; 9−5=4 inches and 5−2=3 inches for the second.
KeyConcepts.Example: Do not subtract edges from unrelated directions.

KeyConcepts.Title: The same solid can be divided in multiple non-overlapping ways
KeyConcepts.Definition: Summing volumes of disjoint rectangular pieces yields the volume of the whole, regardless of a valid horizontal or vertical cut.
KeyConcepts.Example: Draw a boundary and account for every cubic unit exactly once.

KeyConcepts.Title: Volume expressions and units must represent the actual three-dimensional shapes
KeyConcepts.Definition: Three linear factors multiply into cubic units; alternatively base area times perpendicular height yields volume.
KeyConcepts.Example: A calculation of 42 can be correct arithmetically but still not correspond to the student's drawn split.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parentheses describe distinct measured subregions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A grouped product within an addition expression counts one prism's volume, not an unrelated line length.
KeyConcepts.Example: Teacher checks geometric correspondence to the source representation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Figure 1 — missing-foot edges and two splits
WorkedExamples.Question: A measured L-shaped solid is 7 ft across and 7 ft high; its right/lower portion is 5 ft across and 5 ft high; depth is 2 ft. Determine volume.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the labeled source-style dimensions to build an original accessible text-only composite-prism representation, without reusing publisher artwork.
Steps: Compute missing widths/heights from the same orientation: 7−5=2 feet.
Explain why the cuts cover exactly the same solid without overlap.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both partitions give 78 ft³; converting to a different unit without showing conversion is not acceptable.

WorkedExamples.Title: Figure 2 — overhanging-inch solid
WorkedExamples.Question: A measured two-level prism is 9 inches across at its top, 5 inches at its base, 5 inches high including a 2-inch lower level, and 7 inches deep. Find volume in two ways.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the labeled source-style dimensions to build an original accessible text-only composite-prism representation, without reusing publisher artwork.
Steps: Infer overhang length9−5=4 inches and upper height5−2=3 inches.
Verify the overhang and shared depth are not double counted.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each alternative covers the same non-overlapping 259 unit-inch cubes; 259 ft³ would be a unit error.

WorkedExamples.Title: Match parenthesized expressions to prism pieces
WorkedExamples.Question: Interpret the arithmetic ((2×3)×4)+((3×3)×2) and (5×6)+(3×4), and explain what still requires a diagram.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the labeled source-style dimensions to build an original accessible text-only composite-prism representation, without reusing publisher artwork.
Steps: First expression multiplies three perpendicular dimensions for each of two regions:24+18.
Second expression uses one base area times a corresponding height for each region:30+12.
Both totals are42; show how each grouped product corresponds to a non-overlapping piece of the specified figure.
Do not infer geometric equivalence from equal numerical results alone.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both expressions calculate 42 cubic units when attached to an appropriate matching geometry.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher verifies that the actual source diagram's regions, orientation, base/height choices and boundaries match the interpretation.

WorkedExamples.Title: One 420-cubic-inch solid, two decompositions
WorkedExamples.Question: A solid with constant 5-inch depth has a 12-by-6-inch lower rectangle and a 4-by-3-inch top extension. Express its volume two ways.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the labeled source-style dimensions to build an original accessible text-only composite-prism representation, without reusing publisher artwork.
Steps: Demonstrate both decompositions cover identical positions: the 4-inch-wide high section sits beside the 8-inch-wide lower section.
Interpret each parenthesis as one non-overlapping three-dimensional region.
WorkedExamples.Check: The two representations cover the same solid; neither overlaps pieces or drops the top extension.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Subtract dimensions from different axes or assume the hidden edge equals a shown height
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Missing sides are derived only by comparing lengths along the same direction.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the whole and component segments; for example 9−5=4 inches across, 5−2=3 inches high.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Double-count a shared prism overlap, or leave a top extension out
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Two numeric products cannot simply be added unless their represented sub-solids are disjoint and exhaust the shape.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Mark each region once and compare horizontal/vertical voxel sets or a first-party sketch.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Replace cubic feet with cubic inches or generic cubic units
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source's first partner solid uses feet, while the second and 420 example use inches.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Carry ft³ and in³ from each length measurement through all products.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume equal totals prove identical geometric explanations
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 42=42 may occur for two expressions without the student's sketch actually matching the source figure.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher reviews which length/area/height corresponds to every factor and boundary.

SummaryPoints: Use known full lengths and labeled segments in the same direction to find missing edges.
Figure 1 has two valid volume sums 28+50=70+8=78 ft³; Figure 2 has 189+70=175+84=259 in³.
One additional measured source figure has 240+180=360+60=420 in³; both expressions must map to the same solid.
The original partnership requires distinct cuts and organized visual reasoning; grading only totals is insufficient.

Lessons.Title: Represent Volume with Expressions PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: represent the same composite solid's volume with more than one valid expression, including adding non-overlapping prism parts and subtracting a missing rectangular part from a surrounding larger prism.

Warm-up — Notice and Wonder (public source 2021): examine two original text representations of the SAME stepped solid. One shows a yellow lower prism with 10-foot horizontal span and 3-foot depth plus a blue 5-by-3-by-5-foot upper part; the joined solid has overall height 8 feet. The alternate representation cuts vertically rather than horizontally. Ask what is alike or different about their dimensions, and do not equate matching products with identical geometry without checking the shared boundaries.

Activity 1 — compare expressions: in an original example, start with a 5 × 5 × 5 cube and remove a rectangular 2 × 3 × 5 block. The volume is 125−30=95. Alternatively show the same volume as (3 × 5 × 5) + (2 × 2 × 5) = 75+20=95, after verifying those two regions form a disjoint partition of the remaining space.

Activity 2 — source-measured two cuts and subtractive expression: use a 10-foot wide, 8-foot high, 3-foot deep stepped solid. Its right end reaches 4 feet high over 6 feet of width; infer left section width 10−6=4 feet and top extension height 8−4=4 feet. One valid vertical split is (4×8×3)+(6×4×3)=96+72=168 cubic feet. A horizontal split is (10×4×3)+(4×4×3)=120+48=168 cubic feet. Mai's bounding-prism approach is (10×8×3)−(6×4×3)=240−72=168 cubic feet. Have partners DRAW two DIFFERENT non-overlapping partitions and explain why the three equations describe precisely the same occupied region; numerical agreement alone is not enough.

Source and teacher assessment: the 2021 activity first compares 95-cube-unit additive/subtractive expressions, then asks for the 168-ft³ physical shape in two decompositions and a critique of Mai's subtraction. A complete response describes where each factor occurs in the actual drawing, derives unknown lengths (4 feet each), preserves cubic feet and compares strategies. The publicly accessible original 2021 teacher lesson/preparation HTML with embedded Student Facing text was inspected read-only on approved Our-CS; separate Student Task PDF, publisher figures/cards, restricted response and Cool-down remain not independently verified or reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Add disjoint prism pieces
KeyConcepts.Definition: The sum of volumes equals the whole if parts partition it with no gaps or overlap.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Calculate each prism's volume, then add the results.

KeyConcepts.Title: Subtract a missing prism
KeyConcepts.Definition: The occupied region can be a bounding rectangular prism minus an unoccupied rectangular block.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Vremaining = Vbounding − Vmissing only when the missing solid lies entirely inside the bounding solid.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent expressions for the same shape
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two correct decompositions must count exactly the same occupied space.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare the physical regions, not just arithmetic coincidence.

KeyConcepts.Title: Three valid expressions for one measured step solid
KeyConcepts.Definition: The same 10-by-8-by-3-foot bounding region can be represented by two nonoverlapping additive partitions or by subtracting the missing corner.

WorkedExamples.Title: Subtract the empty rectangular part
WorkedExamples.Question: A 5×5×5 cube-shaped region is missing a 2×3×5 rectangular block. What is the remaining volume?
WorkedExamples.Method: Remove the missing block from the bounding cube.
Steps: Compute bounding cube volume: 5×5×5=125.
Compute removed block volume: 2×3×5=30.
Subtract 125−30.
WorkedExamples.Check: Only the specified missing 30 cubes are removed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Add two remaining pieces
WorkedExamples.Question: The same L-shaped solid can be split into a 3×5×5 box and a 2×2×5 box. Find its volume.
WorkedExamples.Method: Sum two disjoint parts.
Steps: Calculate 3×5×5=75.
Calculate 2×2×5=20.
WorkedExamples.Check: The two parts together cover the bounding block except for the original 2×3×5 cut-out.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check another expression
WorkedExamples.Question: A student uses (5×5×5)+(2×3×5) for the cut-out solid. Explain the mistake.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare the sign of the missing piece in the representation.
Steps: Interpret 125 as the volume of the complete bounding cube.
Interpret 30 as an absent region, not an attached region.
Correct the sign to subtraction; recompute 125−30=95.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The valid expression uses subtraction and has volume 95 cubic units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Adding the absent piece would incorrectly count space that is not occupied.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two decompositions of measured prism with inferred 4-foot edges
WorkedExamples.Question: A stepped solid is 10 ft wide, 8 ft high and 3 ft deep; its lower right 6-ft section rises 4 ft. Find two additive volume expressions.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare the same solid as a vertical or a horizontal partition without overlapping regions.
Steps: Infer the left section width: 10−6=4 ft, and extra top height: 8−4=4 ft.
Vertical split: 4×8×3 + 6×4×3 = 96 + 72.
Horizontal split: 10×4×3 + 4×4×3 = 120 + 48.
Compare both partitions and label cubic feet.
WorkedExamples.Check: The two decompositions cover the same three-dimensional occupied cubes without gaps or overlaps, despite using different addends.

WorkedExamples.Title: Explain Mai's bounding subtraction
WorkedExamples.Question: Why does (10×8×3)−(6×4×3) represent the volume of the measured stepped solid?
WorkedExamples.Method: Subtract the unoccupied corner prism from the complete bounding prism.
Steps: The full 10×8×3 bounding box would contain 240 one-foot cubes.
The absent upper right 6×4×3 corner contains 72 one-foot cubes.
Remove the missing 72 to obtain 168, then connect the cut to each additive partition.
WorkedExamples.Check: Subtracting is valid only because the missing prism lies fully inside the bounding box; adding it would be wrong.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Add a removed block as though it were attached
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Empty space in a bounding prism must be subtracted.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label occupied and missing regions before selecting plus or minus.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Write an expression with no geometric partition
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Equal numerical values do not alone certify a shape decomposition.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Show the side lengths and occupied region for each product.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume the second measured shape is just the earlier 95-cube-unit figure
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The 168-ft³ source activity has explicitly different lengths and physical feet units.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Reconstruct from 10,8,6,4 and3 feet and compare the two measured cuts.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Add the missing corner or count an overlapping region twice
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Empty space in a bounding solid is subtracted, while two additive prisms must be disjoint.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use either disjoint partitions or subtract the 72-ft³ missing upper right corner from 240 ft³.

SummaryPoints: A composite solid may be represented by summing disjoint parts or subtracting an empty part from a bounding prism.
Equivalent numerical expressions must correspond to the same volume in cubic units.
For the source-measured figure, 96+72=120+48=240−72=168 ft³; the two missing segments are each 4 ft.
Original student decomposition and justification remain teacher-assessed.

Lessons.Title: All Kinds of Prisms
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: solve real and mathematical volume problems involving packed rectangular prisms and real objects, including dimensions, given base area and composite garden designs. Choose a strategy appropriate to the given information rather than assuming every problem supplies three side lengths.

Warm-up: consider different box-shaped and partially pictured prism figures, describing what information is known and which dimensions would be needed to calculate volume. Multiple justified classifications are valid in the source warm-up.

Activity 1 — prism problems: a storage container 4 feet wide, 9 feet long and 5 feet high has volume 4×9×5 = 180 cubic feet. A walk-in closet with 30 square feet of floor area and a 9-foot ceiling has volume 30×9 = 270 cubic feet, even though the individual floor length and width are not given.

Activity 2 — raised-bed garden: a first-party T-like garden is built by joining non-overlapping rectangular pieces measuring 3 × 8 × 4 feet and 10 × 3 × 4 feet. Compute 96 and 120 cubic feet respectively; combine to 216 cubic feet. Show the location of the dividing plane or explain that the two pieces share only a face.

Assessment: the actual source requires interpreting realistic context, drawing or decomposing a joined garden volume, selecting base area versus edge lengths and justifying the calculation. Numeric Practice alone does not grade the learner's original garden design, reasoning or diagrams. Publisher images and gated Cool-down are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Volume from three dimensions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A packed rectangular prism fills length × width × height cubic units.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply three mutually perpendicular lengths, keeping common units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Volume from given base area
KeyConcepts.Definition: When the floor area is supplied, individual side lengths are not needed to find volume.

KeyConcepts.Title: Volume of joined boxes
KeyConcepts.Definition: A union of disjoint rectangular prisms has the sum of their individual volumes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Separate the solid into parts that share no interior cubic units.
KeyConcepts.Example: 96+120=216 cubic feet for two garden beds.

WorkedExamples.Title: Storage container
WorkedExamples.Question: A box is 4 feet by 9 feet by 5 feet. Find the volume.
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply three linear dimensions.
Steps: Compute base area 4×9=36 square feet.
Multiply by height 5 feet.
Label the result in cubic feet.

WorkedExamples.Title: Closet with known floor area
WorkedExamples.Question: A closet floor covers 30 square feet and its ceiling is 9 feet high. Find its volume.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use provided base area without inventing length/width.
Steps: Recognize 30 square feet is already the base area.
Multiply 30×9.
Attach cubic feet.
WorkedExamples.Check: 30 square feet×9 feet=270 cubic feet.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two-piece raised bed
WorkedExamples.Question: A raised garden uses two joined, non-overlapping 3×8×4 and 10×3×4 foot boxes. What is its total volume?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute both prism volumes and sum them.
Steps: First box: 3×8×4=96 cubic feet.
Second box: 10×3×4=120 cubic feet.
Join only at a face, so add the volumes.
WorkedExamples.Check: 96+120=216; teacher checks the proposed decomposition and design.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Invent a closet length and width
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: When floor area is already known, its separate dimensions are unnecessary.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use square-foot floor area times height.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Count a shared boundary as a volume
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A two-dimensional common face has zero cubic-unit volume.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Add only the non-overlapping interior volumes of the adjoining prisms.

SummaryPoints: Volume problems may provide three edge lengths, a base area plus height, or multiple rectangular components.
Report cubic units and choose a mathematical strategy that matches the given information.
Teacher reviews the garden's physical decomposition, units and explanation.

Lessons.Title: Lots and Lots of Garbage (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: explore how 60 equal-size shipping containers may be arranged in multiple rectangular arrays and reason about their practical placement; then make and justify estimates of container counts on a cargo ship using explicit assumptions. This optional lesson is an authentic modeling/investigation task rather than a unique numeric answer.

Warm-up: discuss the meaning of a ton as a unit of weight and the difference between how much material weighs and how much physical space it occupies. The source discusses about 3,300 tons of plastic trash as context; those mass figures do not by themselves give cubic volume without density or other capacity information.

Activity 1 — sixty containers: give at least five different positive-integer layer arrangements with product 60, for example 1×6×10, 2×5×6, 3×4×5, 2×3×10 and 1×3×20. Sketch or describe each layout, then choose a plausible arrangement for a boat and justify practical considerations such as height, stability and footprint. No layout is automatically 'best' without ship constraints.

Activity 2 — estimating a larger ship: estimate too low, plausible and too high container totals on a partly loaded cargo ship, then refine the estimate for a fuller ship. State assumptions about stacks, rows, columns, containers hidden from view and unusable deck space. Learners can give different valid estimates if assumptions are transparent and calculations follow them.

Assessment and source boundaries: evaluating an argument for a best arrangement, constructing five valid three-factor arrays and critiquing a Fermi-style estimate require teacher review. Automatically grading 60 as the only correct result would erase the original lesson purpose. Source photograph has separate attribution, not copied. Original gated Cool-down not inspected.

KeyConcepts.Title: Array arrangements of sixty
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fixed total can be represented by different factorizations into positive whole-number side counts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For a complete rectangular arrangement, layers × rows × columns = number of containers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Practical constraints
KeyConcepts.Definition: Mathematical volume alone does not determine whether a container layout is safe or desirable.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Consider footprint, height, clearance, support and stability as distinct constraints.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 1×3×20 layout uses 60 containers but may be unsuitable for a particular ship.

KeyConcepts.Title: Defensible modeling estimate
KeyConcepts.Definition: A real-world estimate depends on assumptions about visible and concealed quantities.
KeyConcepts.Rule: State assumptions, compute implied totals, compare bounds and revise when better information appears.
KeyConcepts.Example: If 8 rows × 12 containers per row × 4 vertical layers are assumed, the modeled total is 384.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find five arrangements
WorkedExamples.Question: Produce five different rectangular-array arrangements of 60 identical containers.
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor 60 into three positive integers in different ways.
Steps: Write 1×3×20=60; label which factor is layers, rows or columns.
WorkedExamples.Check: All products are exactly 60; teacher checks the chosen geometry and whether any dimension restrictions apply.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate a container count
WorkedExamples.Question: Assume 8 rows of 12 containers and 4 vertical layers on a rectangular ship section. How many containers are modeled?
WorkedExamples.Method: Make the assumptions explicit and multiply.
Steps: Identify 8×12=96 containers in one complete layer.
Assume exactly four such complete layers.
Multiply 96×4.
WorkedExamples.Check: 384 is not an observed fact about a real ship; changing the assumptions changes the estimate.

WorkedExamples.Title: Critique a best-arrangement claim
WorkedExamples.Question: A group says the tallest possible stack of 60 must be best because it uses all containers. Is that conclusion justified?
WorkedExamples.Method: Distinguish exact container count from practical placement conditions.
Steps: Confirm that a tall stack could still contain exactly 60.
Ask whether the cargo ship has height, weight-distribution or safety limits.
Compare another arrangement with the same count but a lower height.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Not necessarily; both may use 60, and suitability depends on unstated physical constraints.
WorkedExamples.Check: A teacher reviews the proposed justification and what evidence would be needed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat a ton as a cubic-foot unit
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Mass and volume measure different properties and need additional information to convert.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep tons as a weight unit; determine container dimensions and density before making a volume inference.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim one optimal layout without constraints
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Multiple arrays hold the same total, and real-world suitability cannot be inferred from factorization alone.
CommonMistakes.Correction: List assumptions, state safety and footprint constraints, and justify the choice.

SummaryPoints: Sixty identical containers can be arranged in many different rectangular arrays.
Real-world ship container counts and layout decisions depend on explicit assumptions and practical limits.
This optional source investigation is teacher reviewed; no single numeric answer certifies the student task.
